newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan bankruptcy debt hit record high in April.
newsitem.headline: Japan bankruptcy debt hit record high in April.

text.p: A total of 1,432 Japanese companies with a record 2.6 trillion yen ($22.5 billion) in debt went bankrupt in April, led by the biggest Japanese bankruptcy in history, a corporate research form said Thursday.
"Listed companies and over-the-counter companies have been going bankrupt one after another since the beginning of the year," Tokyo Shoko Research Ltd. said in its monthly bankruptcy report.

The main reason for the large increase in debt was the exceptionally large bankruptcies of three nonbank financial firms -- Crown Leasing Corp., Nippon Total Finance Inc. and Nippon Assurance Finance Services Co.
Total debt of the three firms -- all affiliated with troubled long-term credit bank Nippon Credit Bank Ltd. -- was 2.03 trillion yen ($17.5 billion).
Crown Leasing had the largest debt, 1.19 trillion yen ($10.2 billion), which marked the largest bankruptcy ever.
The majority of bankruptcies in April were due to recession-related conditions such as sluggish sales, accumulated losses and unpaid bills, Tokyo Shoko said.

It said the hardest-hit industry was construction, due to increasing competition for orders after a fall in public works spending. Bankruptcies of contractors rose 32.8 percent to 421 cases, up for the seventh consecutive month.
The number of business failures in the wholesale sector was the second-highest and those in manufacturing were the third-highest.
A total of six finance and insurance companies failed in April, up 50 percent from last year.

Tokyo Shoko said it expected bankruptcies to rise further due to Japan's prolonged economic slump and problems of non-performing assets caused by the bursting of Japan's "bubble" of inflated asset prices in the late 1980s.
"There is still a long way to go, considering that the biggest bankruptcy ever took place right at the beginning of the 1997 business year (which started April 1)," Tokyo Shoko said.
